title: One update, 8.5 million screens
teaches: Shipping software and data to a fleet: staged rollouts behind health gates, A/B partitions that fall back, signed updates (TUF and Uptane), deltas and offline devices, compatible versions, and watching fleet health

blocks.text: At 04:09 UTC on Friday 19 July 2024, the security company CrowdStrike sent a configuration file, Channel File 291, to the Falcon software that guards its customers' Windows computers. Falcon reads such files inside the operating system's kernel. This file asked for an input that wasn't there, the code read memory it shouldn't have, and every Windows machine that loaded the file crashed, restarted, loaded it again and crashed again.[^cs] CrowdStrike replaced the file at 05:27 UTC, 78 minutes later. By then Microsoft estimated that about **8.5 million** machines were stuck, including airport check-in desks, hospital systems, broadcasters and payment terminals. A stuck machine couldn't download the fix, because it never stayed up long enough. Administrators had to start each machine by hand in recovery mode to delete the file, and airlines cancelled thousands of flights over the following days.

CrowdStrike treated the file as data rather than code, and sent it to every machine at once without the staged rollout it used for its software. Twelve years earlier, on 1 August 2012, the trading firm Knight Capital had suffered from the opposite error. A technician copied new trading code to seven of its eight servers and missed the eighth. The new code reused a flag that had once switched on an old routine, and on the eighth server that flag woke the old routine, which sent millions of orders into the market. In 45 minutes Knight lost more than $460 million, and within days investors had to rescue the firm.[^knight] CrowdStrike updated its entire fleet at once, while Knight Capital left its fleet running two versions that disagreed about what a flag meant.

In this lesson, we will design an update system for **two million cars** from one maker, each with a computer running its dashboard and navigation, and a few smaller computers beside it. Every month, engineers ship a new software release and a new edition of the map data. You need to deliver both onto the cars without ever leaving a car that won't start, without letting a stolen server key install anything, and at a sensible cost. We will design this system, then compare it with Android, The Update Framework and CrowdStrike's post-incident review.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** Publish a release of software and map data, and offer it to cars in stages, checking each stage's health before proceeding to the next. Halt a release automatically, and undo it on cars that already have it. Install updates without interrupting a car's use, and recover automatically from a release that fails to boot. Prove to each car that a release came from the maker and has not been altered. Update cars that have been parked for months. Ensure the software and map data on each car remain compatible. Display the fleet's health by release, hardware model and region.

**Non-functional.** A faulty release must reach only a small fraction of cars before halting, and no car should ever need a workshop visit to recover from an update. An attacker with one compromised server key must not be able to install anything. Cellular data, which the maker pays for, must cost well under $1 per car per month. 95% of the fleet must receive a release within three weeks.

**Out of scope:** writing the vehicle software, building the map data from surveys (covered in the maps branch, lessons M1 to M4), and providing workshop diagnostic tools for cars broken for other reasons.

A software release is about 1.5 GB and a full edition of the map is about 20 GB, so a full release is 21.5 GB per car, or **43 PB** for the entire fleet. Over cellular at $1 per gigabyte, a round price for bulk data, sending the full release costs $43 million every month, or $21.50 per car. Sending that volume in one day requires about 4 Tb/s of egress bandwidth from the servers. Because the map changes little from month to month, and most of the software does not change at all, our first optimisation is to send only the bytes that changed. You can use the workbench below to see how much bandwidth this saves.

We also need to calculate the failure rates. A defect that stops one car in a thousand from starting will leave 2,000 cars stranded at the roadside if the update reaches the entire fleet. A defect that affects one car in a hundred thousand, or 20 cars in total, might go unnoticed among the fleet's everyday hardware faults. The speed at which a rollout can detect each failure rate determines how we size the stages.

A **staged rollout** offers a release to a small **cohort** first, called the **canary** (after the birds miners carried to warn of toxic gas), monitors its error rates, and expands to larger stages (1%, 10%, 50%, and finally 100%) only if the cohort remains healthy. Consider how that changes the impact of an update as faulty as CrowdStrike's file.

blocks.caption: A release with a defect across a fleet of a million devices, sent all at once or in stages behind a health gate. The vertical axis shows affected devices on a logarithmic scale; the faint line shows the alternative strategy.
blocks.task: Guess, then make the defect rarer until the first stage misses it

blocks.text: In the figure's fleet of one million devices, the first stage catches a severe defect after breaking 2,000 devices instead of 200,000; for a fleet of two million cars, both numbers double. A rarer defect slips through the first stage. At a failure rate of one device in a thousand, the 1% stage causes only 10 additional failures, which is hidden by the fleet's baseline failure rate, making the 10% stage the first cohort large enough to detect the problem. The **health gate** compares the updated cohort with a **control group** of devices running the previous release over the same hours. It matches devices by hardware model and region so that an external disruption, such as a storm or a mobile network outage, is not mistaken for a faulty release. Small initial stages catch common faults with minimal damage, while subsequent larger stages catch rarer faults. A fault too rare for any stage to detect statistically will eventually reach the whole fleet, though slowly enough that engineers or customer support can spot it through bug reports.

The metrics the health gate monitors matter as much as the stage sizes. The gate tracks telemetry reported by the cars, applying the observability metrics of lesson 24 to a fleet: whether the engine started, whether the dashboard software crashed, and whether navigation loaded. Often, the clearest indicator of failure is a lack of data. Because a car stuck in a reboot loop cannot send error reports, the gate tracks expected **heartbeats** from each car and counts missing reports as failures. Engineers select cohorts that include every hardware model and region, because a release that runs cleanly on one hardware revision can break another. Each stage must run long enough for most of its devices to boot and report back. While the figure's six-hour window suits servers that run continuously, a car may sit parked for two days, so stages for a vehicle fleet last two to three days each. If error rates breach the threshold, the gate halts the rollout automatically. Relying on an engineer to read a dashboard at 04:30 is too slow, as CrowdStrike's 78-minute outage demonstrated. As we saw in lesson 23, every change to a fleet, whether code or configuration data, must roll out in stages with a predefined **blast radius** that limits the fraction of the fleet an update can break before automation stops it.

A staged rollout limits how many cars receive a faulty release, but the cars that do receive it must still recover without human intervention, or the maker will have to dispatch a tow truck for each one. We prevent this by changing how the car writes the update to storage.

blocks.caption: Installing an update in place versus writing to the spare partition of a two-slot system with a bootloader that tracks boot attempts.
blocks.task: Use two slots, choose the update that won't boot and play it to the end

blocks.text: With **A/B slots**, the device maintains two complete system partitions. The installer writes the update to the inactive slot while the car operates normally on the active slot, ensuring that an unexpected power loss or an interrupted download leaves the running system intact. Once the write finishes, the installer marks the new slot as bootable. On the next restart, the **bootloader** decrements a retry counter and boots the new slot, which marks itself as permanently valid only after passing its own startup checks. If the new system crashes before passing those checks, the retry counter reaches zero on subsequent restarts and the bootloader falls back to the working slot. Google introduced A/B system updates in Android 7.0 in 2016, using the partition scheme Chromebooks had used since their launch. Doubling the system storage costs very little compared with dispatching a tow truck.

The small computers beside the main one, for the doors or the battery, often have room for only one copy. The main computer then holds the previous version for them, writes the new one, checks it, and writes the old one back if the small computer fails to start.

parts.title: Signed so a stolen key isn't enough

blocks.text: Because an update system can execute arbitrary code on two million cars, it is a high-value target for attackers. Signing every release with a single private key is unsafe, because that key must reside on an online build server to sign routine updates, allowing anyone who compromises the server to push malicious software to the fleet. **The Update Framework** (TUF), published by Justin Samuel, Justin Cappos and colleagues in 2010, divides signing authority across distinct **roles**, each with its own cryptographic keys, so that compromising the online keys used for daily operations cannot compromise the fleet.

blocks.caption: The four roles of The Update Framework, the metadata each role signs, and the order in which a device verifies them.

blocks.text: Engineers keep the **root** keys offline, storing each one inside a hardware security module locked in a safe under the control of a different person. Updating the root metadata requires a threshold of these keyholders to sign together in person with witnesses. The root role specifies which public keys are authorised to sign for the other roles, and can revoke and replace any key that is stolen. The **targets** role lists every update file along with its cryptographic hash and byte size, ensuring that a car rejects any file modified in transit. The **snapshot** role signs the version numbers of all the metadata files in the repository, preventing an attacker from mixing a new targets list with an older one. The **timestamp** role is re-signed automatically every day with a short expiration window, ensuring that if an attacker intercepts traffic and feeds a car outdated metadata, the car detects the stale timestamp within 24 hours. Finally, metadata version numbers must increase monotonically, so an attacker cannot replay a legitimately signed older release to reintroduce a patched vulnerability.[^rollback] Consequently, rolling back a buggy release that cars have already marked as valid requires rolling forward: engineers rebuild the previous working code as release 43 with an incremented version number, and deploy it through an accelerated staged rollout.

Cars added a problem of their own: a car has many computers, and each must get the right image for its exact part number. **Uptane**, an adaptation of TUF for cars developed from 2016, splits the server side in two. An **image repository**, signed with offline keys, holds every image. A **director**, online, tells each car which images it should install. A car installs an image only if both agree, so a stolen director key can at worst choose among genuine images, and a stolen image key can't send anything without the director.[^uptane]

Next, we must manage the bandwidth and data costs. In the model below, you can choose whether to send full releases or **deltas** (binary patches containing only the bytes that changed since the car's current version); whether cars wait to download over home Wi-Fi and fall back to cellular after two weeks, or download over cellular immediately; how many previous releases you generate deltas for; and how many days to spread the rollout across. Assume 70% of cars connect to Wi-Fi at home, and 3% sit parked with the ignition off for months at a time.

blocks.caption: Simulating a monthly release to two million cars. Line thickness represents data volume, using representative bulk pricing for bandwidth.
blocks.task: Keep cellular under $1 million a month, the peak under 100 Gb/s, and 95% within three weeks

blocks.text: Sending deltas provides the largest reduction in data volume. A car running last month's release downloads 1.15 GB instead of 21.5 GB, a 95% reduction, because a monthly map update modifies only a small percentage of map tiles and a software update modifies only a fraction of the binaries. Preferring Wi-Fi shifts most of the remaining traffic off the metered cellular network, though cars without home Wi-Fi must wait two weeks before downloading the update. Spreading the rollout announcements over several days reduces peak server egress bandwidth, and aligns naturally with the multi-day stages of the health gate without extending the total rollout schedule.

Long-term parked cars determine how many historical versions we must support. A car started after five months at an airport car park is five releases behind the fleet. Because engineers must build, store and test a separate delta file for each supported starting version, we only generate deltas from the last few releases; any car running an older version downloads the full 21.5 GB release instead. When a car connects and reports that it is running software version 38 and map version 2026.06, the update server calculates the lowest-cost verified upgrade path, returning either a single delta, a sequential chain of deltas, or the full image. Furthermore, because roughly 2% of the fleet remains on older releases even a month after a rollout, every backend API the cars communicate with must maintain backwards compatibility across all active versions.

Suppose that in November the mapping team publishes a map edition using a new file format, version 8, which adds detailed lane geometry. Software release 42 includes the parser for format 8, whereas release 41 supports only format 7. The map update rolls out in stages behind a health gate, and within the 1% canary cohort, the 20% of cars still running software release 41 attempt to load the format 8 map, fail to parse it, and display a blank navigation screen. Those cars report map-loading errors in their daily heartbeats, causing the health gate to detect a failure rate much higher than the control group's and halt the rollout after affecting only a few thousand cars, each of which falls back to the format 7 map stored in its inactive partition.

We prevent this failure by enforcing version compatibility on the server. The update server must never offer a car a map format that its currently installed software cannot parse. Because every update request from a car includes its active software version, the server responds to cars on release 41 with the newest map compiled in format 7. The mapping pipeline continues compiling new maps in both format 7 and format 8 until fewer than 1% of the fleet remains on release 41, while offering those lagging cars a combined update containing software release 42 and the format 8 map. In distributed systems, deploying code that reads a new format before deploying code that writes it is called the **expand and contract** pattern: first add support for the new format alongside the old one (expand), wait until all clients have upgraded to read the new format, and only then stop generating the old format (contract). By ensuring every car can parse format 8 before sending format 8 data, we avoid the version mismatch that brought down Knight Capital. Any flag, API field or file format must retain its exact meaning for as long as any device in the fleet still reads it, and any breaking change requires a new version identifier.

Each car transmits a **heartbeat** message once a day or whenever the ignition starts, reporting its current software and map versions, its hardware model, the number of boots and crashes since the last report, and any failed self-tests. Because the car maintains these metrics as local counters and transmits only the cumulative totals in a payload of a few hundred bytes, two million cars generate less than 1 GB of telemetry per day, which easily succeeds even over poor cellular connections. If a car drives out of cellular coverage for a week, its next heartbeat simply reports the accumulated totals for the entire week. Because a car's internal clock may drift if its battery disconnects, the ingestion server records both the car's local timestamp and the server's reception timestamp.

The telemetry servers aggregate these heartbeats into time-series counters grouped by **cohort**: software release, map edition, hardware model and geographic region. Both the automated health gate and human operators query these aggregates. An engineering dashboard plots each cohort's crash rate alongside its matching control group, allowing an operator to drill down from an overall release to a specific hardware model, country, and list of affected vehicles, and then pull detailed diagnostic logs from an individual car on demand, avoiding the prohibitive cellular cost of uploading full debug logs from the entire fleet every day. Automated alerts trigger based on the **burn rate** introduced in lesson 24, which measures how quickly a cohort consumes its monthly error budget relative to a constant baseline rate. Given an error budget where at most 0.1% of vehicle starts may fail over 30 days, a burn rate of 14.4 consumes 2% of the monthly budget in a single hour and pages an on-call engineer immediately, whereas a slower burn rate sustained over six hours opens a bug ticket.[^burn]

In their post-incident review published in August 2024, CrowdStrike announced that rapid-response content updates like Channel File 291 would henceforth deploy in concentric rings starting with a canary cohort, gated by automated health checks and customer opt-in controls, and that the Falcon sensor would validate the bounds of all input fields before executing a template. In short, CrowdStrike applied the same deployment pipeline to configuration data that it already used for compiled code. Consumer operating systems update hundreds of millions of phones and laptops using the exact mechanisms we have designed: Android uses A/B partitions and staged rollouts via Google Play, while ChromeOS combines dual root partitions with verified boot signatures. Package managers such as Python's PyPI and container registries use TUF to secure software distribution, and automotive manufacturers deploy Uptane to secure connected vehicles.

The failure at Knight Capital led to stricter automated deployment practices across the software industry. Modern deployment pipelines push releases to every server automatically rather than relying on manual file copies, run configuration management agents that continuously verify that every server's running state matches the target manifest, and delete deprecated code paths and feature flags from the codebase rather than leaving them dormant.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **Ten times**, twenty million cars, is mostly more of the same. Deltas over a CDN scale with the CDN; heartbeats grow to a few gigabytes a day, still small. What grows is the version matrix: more models, more years of cars in the field, each needing its own images and its own cohorts. The release system has to treat "which image for which car" as data, a table keyed by part number and version, built and tested automatically.

**A hundred times**, two hundred million devices, is the size of a phone platform. The servers answering "what should I install" must answer from precomputed tables per cohort, without touching a database per device. The bytes go partly between devices, as Windows' Delivery Optimization lets computers on the same network share update pieces, and through caches inside internet providers. And the stages slow down: a defect affecting one device in a million is 200 devices, and finding it takes a cohort of millions watched for days.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on getting an update safely onto a fleet
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: CrowdStrike's Channel File 291 reached about 8.5 million machines within 78 minutes. What change to how it was released would most have limited the damage?
choices: Releasing it in stages from a small cohort, halting automatically when that cohort's machines stopped reporting
Writing the replacement file more quickly, so that the fix could have been sent within minutes of the first crash
Sending the file only to the machines that had been restarted in the last day, which were known to be healthy
items.why: A configuration file can break machines as easily as compiled code. A first stage of 1% would have stopped the rollout with a hundredth of the machines affected, and stricter bounds checking of the file's inputs inside the sensor would have prevented the crash.

items.ask: A defect breaks one device in a thousand. A 1% stage of a million-device fleet shows nothing unusual. Why?
choices: The health gate checks only for crashes, and this defect must be causing something other than a crash
Ten extra failures among 10,000 devices are hidden by the ordinary background failures
Defects that rare can only be found in the lab, before release
items.why: Each stage detects only faults frequent enough to stand out above the fleet's baseline failure rate. Detecting rarer faults requires larger sample sizes, which is why each subsequent stage is larger than the last.

items.ask: Why does a health gate compare the cohort with a control group instead of with a fixed threshold?
choices: So that a bad day for every device, such as a network outage, isn't blamed on the release
Because a control group of devices is needed to roll the release back if the health gate halts it
Because a fixed threshold would need the whole fleet's data before it could be set to a sensible value
items.why: Updated and un-updated devices experience the same weather, network outages and time-of-day traffic patterns; only the software release differs between them.

items.ask: A car with A/B slots installs an update that crashes as it starts. What happens?
choices: The car stays broken until the next release fixes it
The car downloads the old version again over cellular, installs it over the new one and restarts
The bootloader sees the failed start and boots the old slot again
items.why: The new system partition marks itself valid only after passing its startup health checks; until then, the bootloader falls back to the untouched working partition if the new one fails to boot.

items.ask: An attacker steals the online key that signs TUF's timestamp role. What can they do?
choices: Sign and install any software they like on every device that trusts the repository
Freeze devices on old releases for a while, but install nothing new
Replace the root keys with keys of their own, and from then on control every role
items.why: With the timestamp key alone, an attacker can re-sign old timestamp metadata to keep devices from seeing new updates until the snapshot or targets metadata expires, but they cannot alter any files because the file hashes are signed by offline keys.

items.ask: A car parked for five months comes back. Deltas exist only from the last three releases. What should it get?
choices: The latest delta, applied to whatever version the car happens to have installed
Nothing until it has been taken to a workshop and updated there by hand, from a cable
The cheapest tested path from its versions: a chain of deltas, or the full release
items.why: A binary delta applies cleanly only to the exact byte sequence it was generated from, so the update server selects either a verified chain of deltas or a full image based on the car's current versions.

items.ask: A new map format can't be read by last month's software. How should the map be released?
choices: Release the map to every car first, and the software that reads it a week later
Software that reads both formats first, and the old map kept for cars not yet updated
Release both on the same day, so that the map and the software arrive at each car together
items.why: Because cars download updates at different times, the server must send each car a map format compatible with its currently installed software until almost the entire fleet has upgraded to the new reader.

summary: **Data is code.** A configuration file or a map edition can break a fleet just like compiled software, and requires the same staged rollout.

**Stage every change behind a health gate.** Roll out to 1%, 10%, 50%, and finally 100% of the fleet while monitoring health metrics; small stages catch common faults while larger stages catch rare ones.
**Compare with a control group, count the silent.** Compare updated devices against un-updated devices over the same time window, and count missing heartbeats as failures.
**Halt automatically.** A bad update can brick a fleet in 78 minutes, which is faster than human operators can spot a trend on a dashboard.
**Install into a spare slot.** Using A/B partitions and a bootloader with a retry counter allows a device to fall back automatically if an update fails to boot.

**Split signing trust.** TUF separates keys by role to keep root and targets keys offline, expires stale metadata, and enforces monotonically increasing version numbers; Uptane adds a director repository for multi-controller vehicles.
**Send differences, on cheap networks, spread out.** Binary deltas, Wi-Fi preference and staggered rollouts reduce bandwidth volume, cellular data costs and peak server load.
**Every version in the field must keep working.** Deploy new readers before new writers, never repurpose existing flags, and serve each device only formats its current software supports.

cs.title: Channel File 291
cs.text: CrowdStrike's root cause analysis, published in August 2024, explained that the IPC template type defined 21 input fields, whereas the sensor's template interpreter passed only 20 inputs. Earlier Channel Files of that type had used wildcard matching on the 21st field, but Channel File 291 inspected the 21st input directly, causing an out-of-bounds memory read in the Windows kernel.

knight.title: Power Peg
knight.text: According to the SEC's enforcement order of October 2013, the legacy routine was called Power Peg, which Knight had stopped using in 2003 but never deleted from the codebase. The new Retail Liquidity Program code repurposed the configuration flag that had previously activated Power Peg. Because engineers had removed the cumulative-quantity check from the Power Peg execution path years earlier, the eighth server continuously submitted child orders for parent orders that were already filled. During the outage, Knight's engineers rolled back the new code on the other seven servers while leaving the flag enabled, causing all eight servers to execute Power Peg.

rollback.title: Fallback and anti-rollback
rollback.text: A/B partition fallback and anti-rollback protection do not conflict because they trigger at different stages of the boot process. Until the newly updated slot passes its health checks and marks itself as verified, the previous slot remains the highest verified version on the device, so the bootloader is permitted to boot it. Once the new slot marks itself verified, the system increments a minimum version counter, often stored in one-time programmable hardware fuses, and henceforth refuses to boot any image with a lower version number.

uptane.title: Uptane in a car
uptane.text: In Uptane a car's main computer does the full checks for both repositories and passes images to the smaller computers. Those that can afford it check the signatures again themselves; the smallest check only a few. Each computer reports what it is running, signed, so the director can see a car's real state rather than what it was told to install.

burn.title: Burn rates for a fleet
burn.text: Given a 30-day error budget of 0.1% failed starts, a cohort experiencing a 1.44% failure rate for one hour consumes 2% of its monthly budget in that hour, corresponding to a burn rate of 14.4 (the fast-burn paging threshold recommended in Google's SRE Workbook). The workbook pairs this immediate page with a slower alert threshold at a burn rate of 6 sustained over six hours, which consumes 5% of the monthly budget. Engineers can apply the same error-budget arithmetic to any fleet telemetry metric, including failed installations, partition fallbacks or missing heartbeats.
